title: From Your Hand to the Edge of the Universe
lines: This is a human hand. | About ten centimeters across.
Now let's zoom out, ten times wider at every step, | until we reach the edge of everything we can see.
A person, lying in the grass on a summer afternoon.
A blanket, a few trees, and a footpath.
This is the Sheep Meadow, | in New York's Central Park.
The park is four kilometers long, | a green rectangle cut out of the city grid.
Manhattan: an island twenty-one kilometers long, | home to more than one and a half million people.
The whole city, | wrapped around one of the largest natural harbors in the world.
The east coast of North America, | and the curve of the planet starts to show.
The Earth. | Twelve thousand seven hundred kilometers across.
The International Space Station orbits just four hundred kilometers up, | barely above the surface at this scale.
The Moon, | three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away. | Light makes the trip in just over a second.
Only a handful of humans have ever traveled this far from home.
The Sun. | A hundred and fifty million kilometers away. | Its light takes about eight minutes to reach us.
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars: | the rocky inner planets, | and past them, the asteroid belt.
Then the giants: | Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, | and Neptune, four and a half billion kilometers out.
Voyager 1, launched in nineteen seventy-seven, | is the farthest object humans have ever built. | It's nearly a full light-day away.
A light-year is nearly ten trillion kilometers. | Around the Sun, the {Oort~Ort} cloud may hold trillions of icy comets, | stretching more than a light-year out.
Four light-years away: | Proxima Centauri, the nearest star. | Voyager would need more than seventy thousand years to get there.
Within ten light-years, | there are only about a dozen stars.
Nearly every star you can see at night | lies within a few thousand light-years.
The Milky Way. | A hundred thousand light-years across, | with hundreds of billions of stars.
We're out here, in a quiet arm, twenty-six thousand light-years from the center. | There, a black hole four million times heavier than the Sun sits waiting.
The Sun takes about two hundred thirty million years to go around once. | The last time we were here, | the first dinosaurs were just appearing.
The Local Group: | the Milky Way, Andromeda, | and dozens of smaller galaxies.
Andromeda is two and a half million light-years away. | On a dark night you can see it with your naked eye, | as light that set off long before our species existed.
Galaxies gather in groups, | groups into clusters, | and clusters into superclusters.
Ours is called {Laniakea~Lahnia-Kayah}, Hawaiian for immense heaven: | about a hundred thousand galaxies, | spread across five hundred million light-years.
Zoom out again, | and the galaxies line up into filaments and walls, | around enormous empty voids. | The cosmic web.
Every point of light here is a galaxy.
The observable universe. | Ninety-three billion light-years across, | holding hundreds of billions of galaxies.
The universe is thirteen point eight billion years old, | but space has been stretching the whole time, | so the farthest light we see came from places that are now much farther away.
At the edge is the oldest light there is: | the afterglow of the Big Bang.
Beyond it, light hasn't had time to reach us yet. | Nobody knows how far the universe really goes.
And since light reaches us from every direction at the same speed, | the center of the observable universe | is right where you are.
So let's go back.
A human hand. | About twenty-eight steps of ten | from the edge of everything we can see.
Let's zoom out.
